claims.text: HfNbTiVAl10 has been reported in a hierarchical heterostructured state with multilevel chemical fluctuations and phase heterogeneities.
High-resolution in situ TEM and EBSD can quantify phase contrast, local crystallographic orientation, and defect density during tensile and fracture experiments.
Targeted microscale tensile and fracture tests can validate whether imaging-derived descriptors capture failure-relevant features.
The proposed imaging and calibration protocol will yield robust, quantifiable microstructural descriptors.
Multilevel chemical fluctuations and heterostructural morphology parameters mediate the mechanical response of HfNbTiVAl10.
Machine-learning algorithms can map validated imaging-derived descriptors to Young's modulus, yield strength, and toughness.
Imaging-derived descriptors can serve as surrogates for the alloy's intrinsic elastic and plastic responses.
Subtle mesoscale damage initiation governs fracture toughness in this alloy.
Direct descriptor-to-property machine learning can bypass computationally intensive CALPHAD and first-principles approaches.
The proposed method will reduce prediction errors for Young's modulus, yield strength, and toughness by 20–30% relative to current simulation-based methods.
The proposed method will improve efficiency by 5–10 times relative to existing CALPHAD and first-principles approaches.
Existing CALPHAD, first-principles, and simulation-feature-based machine-learning approaches have high computational demands.
Existing simulation-based approaches have limited predictive capability for fracture toughness.

The method is expected to remain reliable under controlled strain rates and temperatures no higher than approximately 300 °C when periodic mechanical calibration confirms descriptor-property correlations.
Extreme strain rates, temperatures beyond the calibrated range, or insufficient imaging resolution may compromise prediction accuracy.
Nonlinear scaling of microscale failure features may reduce predictive performance outside the calibrated regime.
A blinded prospective comparison of model predictions with standard tensile and fracture-toughness measurements can test the method.
The hypothesis will be considered falsified if prediction errors consistently exceed 30% or if imaging descriptors are not significantly correlated with microcrack initiation and progression.
